title: The Evidence for Evolution
hook: Fossils, DNA, shared body plans, and change we can watch happen — evolution isn't a hunch, it's a conclusion forced by many independent lines of evidence.
key_points: Fossils record a sequence of past life, with transitional forms linking groups.
DNA comparisons show all life is related, with closer kin sharing more sequence.
Shared anatomy — like the same bones in a bat wing, whale flipper, and human arm — points to common ancestry.
Evolution is observed directly, from antibiotic-resistant bacteria to finch beaks.
content_html: Ask why biologists are so confident about evolution and the answer is that the evidence comes from many directions at once, and it all points the same way. The fossil record lays out a rough sequence of life through time, complete with transitional forms — feathered dinosaurs, walking-whale ancestors — that bridge major groups. Living bodies tell the same story: the bones in a bat's wing, a whale's flipper, and your own arm are the same set, just reshaped.
extra_html: The strongest modern confirmation comes from DNA. When we read the genomes of different species, closely related ones share more sequence, producing a branching family tree that independently matches the one drawn from fossils and anatomy. And evolution isn't only a story about the deep past — we watch it happen, from bacteria evolving resistance to antibiotics within years to finch beaks shifting with drought. UC Berkeley's Understanding Evolution project lays out how these separate lines of evidence converge, which is what makes the case so hard to escape: each could stand alone, but together they leave little room for doubt.

related.title: Natural Selection
related.hook: No designer, no goal — just heritable variation, a struggle to survive, and the slow accumulation of whatever happens to work. That's how life adapts.

related.title: The Tree of Life
related.hook: Humans, mushrooms, and oak trees share an ancestor if you go back far enough — all life on Earth branches from a single common root.

related.title: How New Species Form
related.hook: Split one population in two, let them drift apart long enough, and eventually they can no longer interbreed — that's speciation, the engine that fills the tree of life with branches.

flashcards.prompt: Why does the same bone arrangement appear in a bat's wing, a whale's flipper, and a human arm?

choices.text: They inherited the limb plan from a shared ancestor
Each evolved it independently from scratch for the same job
It's a coincidence with no biological meaning

flashcards.explanation_html: These are homologous structures — the same underlying bones repurposed for different uses, which makes sense only if all three descend from a common ancestor.

flashcards.prompt: Name four independent lines of evidence for evolution.
flashcards.back_html: The fossil record, DNA/molecular comparisons, shared anatomy (homologies), and directly observed change in living populations.

flashcards.prompt: What do DNA comparisons reveal about different species?

choices.text: Closely related species share more of their DNA sequence
Every species has completely unique, unrelated DNA
DNA is identical across all living things

flashcards.explanation_html: The more recently two species shared an ancestor, the more similar their DNA — a nested pattern that matches the tree of life built from fossils and anatomy.
